name: Hafiz Ibrahim
bio: Muhammad Hafiz ibn Ibrahim Fahmi was born in 1287 AH (1871 CE) on a dahabiya, a Nile houseboat, moored at Dayrut; his father died while he was small, and an uncle brought him up. He graduated from the military school in 1891 and went with the Sudan campaign, was later put on the reserve list and turned to Sheikh Muhammad Abduh, and in 1911 became head of the literary section of the Egyptian National Library, where he stayed until shortly before his death. Called the Poet of the Nile, and by al-Zirikli “Egypt's national poet”, he wrote on the nation, on society and on public occasions, translated two parts of Victor Hugo's Les Misérables and wrote Layali Satih. When the poets crowned Ahmad Shawqi Prince of Poets in 1927, it was Hafiz who declared the pledge: “Prince of rhymes, I have come to pledge allegiance.” He died in Cairo in 1351 AH (1932 CE).
